blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — clinical alarm management
stem: A monitored client's usual heart rate remains above the unit's default high-alarm threshold. Which approach best supports alarm safety?

options.A: Reassess the client and, within approved policy, tailor the alarm limit to the individual's clinical baseline while preserving a threshold that signals meaningful change.
options.B: Leave the default limit unchanged even when it repeatedly produces nonactionable alarms, because individualized alarm settings reduce safety.
options.C: Silence the heart-rate alarm for the remainder of the shift after confirming the client's current rate is expected for that client.
options.D: Disable physiologic alarms whenever a chronic abnormal baseline is documented, then rely on periodic manual vital-sign checks for deterioration.

rationale: A is correct. AHRQ patient-safety guidance identifies alarm settings that are not tailored to the individual patient as a contributor to alarm fatigue and recommends configuring alarms to the patient's own baseline at a clinically actionable level, while following institutional policy. B promotes repeated nonactionable alarms. C and D remove clinically meaningful alerting rather than improving alarm specificity.
educational_objective: Apply individualized, policy-consistent physiologic alarm settings that reduce nonactionable alarms while preserving clinically meaningful alerts.
source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ); NCSBN
source_document_title: Harm From Alarm Fatigue; Reducing the Safety Hazards of Monitor Alert and Alarm Fatigue; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: Current AHRQ PSNet alarm-safety resources live-rechecked 2026-08-21; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: AHRQ Harm From Alarm Fatigue: non-individualized default settings contribute to alarm fatigue; clinicians can tailor alarm settings for individual patients when defaults do not fit; alarms should not be completely silenced. AHRQ alarm-fatigue perspective: once adequate patient data are available, configure alarm limits to the individual's own normal at a level where action/intervention is required, consistent with hospital policy.
source_claim_supported: AHRQ directly supports individualized clinically actionable alarm thresholds and rejects complete silencing as a response to recurrent nonactionable alarms.

pdf_visual_verification: PASS — relevant official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan safety page was screenshot-verified earlier in this continuation; alarm-management claims rely on AHRQ HTML.

option_audit.A: Correct; preserves meaningful monitoring while individualizing the threshold within policy.
option_audit.B: Plausible standardization argument but repeated nonactionable defaults contribute to alarm fatigue.
option_audit.C: Plausible nuisance-alarm shortcut but removes the safety function rather than tailoring it.
option_audit.D: Plausible chronic-baseline workaround but disables physiologic alerting and creates avoidable risk.

cueing_audit.answer_length: All options are comparable in clinical detail and structure; the key is not uniquely signaled by length.
cueing_audit.absolute_words: No distractor depends on simplistic always/never/only wording.
